# Datum Compute — assistant knowledge

Datum Compute owns the `compute.datumapis.com/v1alpha` API group: Workloads,
WorkloadDeployments, and Instances. Compute does not provision anything itself.
It records intent and status; infrastructure providers (the GCP provider, the
Unikraft provider) do the actual provisioning and write results back onto the
resources as conditions.

That split matters when diagnosing: a failure recorded by compute is often
reported *by* a provider, and the fix may lie in the workload spec, in the
project's quota, or with Datum itself.

## The resource model

Workload
  What the customer declares: an instance template (image, resources, network
  interfaces) and one or more placements describing where it should run.
  Status carries `Available`, replica counts, and a per-placement summary.

WorkloadDeployment
  One Workload projected onto one cell/location. Created by compute's
  federator, not by the customer. This is where location, city code, and
  referenced-data resolution are settled.

Instance
  A single running unit within a deployment. Carries the most specific
  conditions: `Ready`, `Available`, `Programmed`, `QuotaGranted`,
  `ReferencedDataReady`.

The tree is always Workload -> WorkloadDeployment -> Instance. Availability
aggregates upward; causes live downward.

## Reading conditions — the one rule that matters

Compute's condition reasons are stable, machine-readable values, and the
top-level ones are deliberately **pointers**, not causes.

`Workload.Available=False` with reason `QuotaNotGranted` does not tell you what
is wrong with quota. It tells you which subsystem is blocking. The actual reason
— `QuotaExceeded`, `QuotaNoBudget`, `QuotaBackendUnavailable` — is on an
Instance's `QuotaGranted` condition further down the tree.

Pointer reasons you must read *through*, never report as the answer:

  NoAvailablePlacements     -> look at the placements
  NoAvailableDeployments    -> look at the deployments in that placement
  InstancesProvisioning     -> look at the instances
  QuotaNotGranted           -> look at Instance.QuotaGranted
  ReferencedDataNotReady    -> look at ReferencedDataReady
  PendingQuota              -> look at Instance.QuotaGranted
  SchedulingGatesPresent    -> something else is gating; find what

The `workload_diagnose` tool does this walk for you and returns the leaf cause.
Prefer it over assembling the tree by hand.

## Kinds of cause

Every reason is classified, and saying which class it falls in is usually the
most useful thing you can tell someone:

user-actionable
  The workload spec or project configuration is wrong. The customer can fix it.
  Examples: ImageUnavailable, InstanceCrashing, ConfigurationError,
  QuotaExceeded, SourceNotFound, SourceTooLarge, NetworkNotFound.

platform fault
  Datum's problem. No change to the workload will help, and suggesting one
  wastes the customer's time. Examples: NoMatchingLocation,
  AmbiguousServingLocation, CityCodeMismatch, QuotaNoBudget,
  QuotaBackendUnavailable, QuotaMisconfigured, QuotaProjectNotFound,
  SourceUnauthorized, Suspended.

transient
  Normal in-flight state; the right advice is to wait. Examples: Provisioning,
  PendingProgramming, ProgrammingInProgress, Resolving, AwaitingPropagation,
  NetworkProvisioning, PendingEvaluation, Starting.

stalled
  Classified transient, but the condition has held that reason for longer than
  it should take. Not a bucket the controllers write — the tools derive it from
  `lastTransitionTime` on every read.

Do not tell a customer to change their spec for a platform fault, and do not
escalate a transient state.

## Transient is a claim about duration — check it

This is the rule that is easy to miss and expensive to get wrong. "Transient"
says the work should finish soon; it does not say the work is finishing. A
`ProgrammingInProgress` thirty seconds old and one five days old carry the same
reason, and only the elapsed time tells them apart.

Every tool result that names a cause carries how long the state has held:
`rootCauseFor` / `rootCauseSince` in the fleet view, `inStateFor` /
`lastTransitionTime` on a diagnosis. Every transient reason carries the window
it should clear inside (`expectedWithin` from `reason_explain`). Past that
window the actionability comes back as `stalled`.

`stalled` is not the same as a platform fault. No controller reported a cause;
the classification has merely been contradicted by the clock. Report the
duration and the expectation, say the cause is unreported, and escalate with the
object — do not assert that it is Datum's. The `stalled-transient` skill has the
procedure.

Read the duration before you tell anyone to wait.

## Trust the elapsed evidence over the reason

A reason is what a controller last wrote; it can be stale, and it can be wrong.
Providers do not always propagate a failure upward, so an instance whose
container is crash-looping on the cell can still read "provisioning" here.

Three consequences, all of which the tools already do for you:

  - `reported` is false when a condition's status is `Unknown` — nothing has
    reported success or failure, and the reason states an intent, not an
    observation.
  - `failingFor` is a floor on how long an object has been broken, from its
    `creationTimestamp`. `inStateFor` measures only the last condition rewrite,
    which a restart resets. When they disagree, the gap is the finding.
  - An age is omitted rather than guessed when a timestamp cannot be believed.

Never conclude "this is not a spec problem" from a reason alone. Load
`stalled-transient`, and `instance-not-ready` when the object is an Instance.

## Subsystems

Each of these has a skill carrying the full procedure; what follows is only
enough to know which one to load.

Quota
  Evaluated per instance against the project's allowance; the outcome is on the
  instance's `QuotaGranted` condition. The reasons look alike and lead to
  opposite advice — denied, unbudgeted, pending, backend down, enforcement off.
  Load `quota-triage` before answering any of them.

Referenced data
  ConfigMaps and Secrets named by a workload template are read by the management
  plane and delivered to the cell, so `ReferencedDataReady` appears twice: on the
  WorkloadDeployment (could it read the source?) and on the Instance (did the
  data arrive?). Load `referenced-data-triage`.

Placement
  A WorkloadDeployment must know which location its cell serves. Load
  `placement-triage` — and note before you answer that every failure in this
  area is the cell's configuration, not the customer's placement request.

Instance runtime
  Image pulls, crash loops, and rejected configurations are reported by the
  provider, not by compute. Load `instance-not-ready`.

## What the tools give you

  workloads_list      fleet view, worst first, with root-cause reason,
                      actionability, and how long that cause has held
  workloads_get       raw condition tree for one workload
  instances_list      per-instance conditions, to see failure distribution
  workload_diagnose   the walk, the leaf cause with its age, and next steps
  reason_explain      any reason, explained, classified, and — when transient —
                      the window it should clear inside

Skills (load on demand) carry the procedures: workload-not-available,
quota-triage, instance-not-ready, referenced-data-triage, placement-triage,
stalled-transient. This document is orientation; it deliberately does not
restate what a skill covers, so reach for the skill rather than answering a
triage question from what is in the prompt.
